name: Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough-juxta-Penarth — central case chronology

events.event: St Dochdwy’s, beside the farm, thought to be an early monastery (archaeology)
Robert Fitzhamon grants lands including Llandough to Tewkesbury Abbey (prior of St Mary's, Cardiff becomes lord of the manor) — per a 2011 Penarth Times letter, not a primary source.

Charters printed by G. T. Clark (Cartae, vol. I, pp.181–184, from BL Additional Charters 24.287–24.290) record persons surnamed de Landoch dealing in property in Landoch. CXCIX grants a messuage on the south side of the church of St Doguin, next to the cemetery, held of the abbot and convent of Tewkesbury at 4d a year. The charters name no house; their dating is not checked.
events.source: G. T. Clark (ed.), Cartae et alia munimenta, vol. I (Dowlais, 1885), pp.181–184, Internet Archive copy

events.event: The Annals of Tewkesbury for 1238, as summarised by D. R. Paterson (1934, p. 28), record a dispute over Cogan chapel after which it "remained in its first condition, as it is, a chapel of Llandough"; a presentation of 1184-5 had already named Llandough as the mother church (EV-0842). The Annals themselves are not checked.
events.source: D. R. Paterson, 'The Manors of Sully, Cosmeston, Penarth and Cogan', Trans. Cardiff Naturalists' Society LXVII (1934), pp. 17-30 (NLW Welsh Journals scan, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: The Valor Ecclesiasticus shows the manor of Llandough belonging to the Abbot of Tewkesbury, "who there had free and villein tenants paying rents of assize", as summarised by the editor of Cardiff Records vol. 2 (1900) (EV-0825). The 1535 return itself is not checked.
events.source: J. Hobson Matthews (ed.), Cardiff Records vol. 2 (1900), pp. 8-41 (British History Online, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: John Leland's Itinerary lists "Pont Lecwith of 3. [arches] of stone" among the bridges on the Ely, and passes "Cogan Pille ... wher is a fair maner place on the ripe side longging to Mr. Herebert of Swansey, and then to Ponte Lecwith of stone scant a mile" (1906 edition, pp. 19, 25; EV-0830). Coflein dates a stone bridge here "as early as 1536" (EV-0828). The manuscript is not checked.
events.source: The Itinerary in Wales of John Leland, ed. L. Toulmin Smith (1906), archive.org copy

events.event: King Henry VIII grants Llandough manor to Lord Clynton and Say and Robert Turwitt; by 1545 it has been acquired by Sir George Herbert, "as appears by a rent-roll of that date", as summarised by the editor of Cardiff Records vol. 2 (1900) (EV-0825). A grant of a manor (lordship) is not a grant of freehold in any farm; the grant and the rent-roll are not checked.
events.source: J. Hobson Matthews (ed.), Cardiff Records vol. 2 (1900), pp. 8-41 (British History Online, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: Rice Merrick's Morganiae Archaiographia places Pennarth, Cogan, Landoch and Leckwith in the hundred of Dynispowys, and its ploughland table gives "Cogan iiij" and "East Landoch & Penarch iij", with Leckwith listed (1887 edition, pp. 44, 108-109; EV-0832). The "East Landoch" form marks this Llandough apart from Llandough near Cowbridge. The manuscript is not checked.
events.source: Rice Merrick, A Booke of Glamorganshires Antiquities (1578; Dryden Press, 1887), archive.org copy

events.event: The Herbert Abbreviate records that the manor of "Landoche-juxta-Cardif had free tenants, demesnes and copyholds", and that Leckwith manor "hath free tenants leases, coppy houlds, and customary lands and tenaunts to them and theire heires for ever", as printed in Cardiff Records vol. 2 (1900) (EV-0825). The manuscript is not checked.
events.source: J. Hobson Matthews (ed.), Cardiff Records vol. 2 (1900), pp. 8-41 (British History Online, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: James Corey, clerk, is admitted by Bishop Hugh of Llandaff to the rectory of "Lickwith, Landough et Cogan" on the death of Thomas Basset, on the presentation of William Herbert, esquire, "true patron" (William Herbert of the White Friars in Cardiff) (Bishops' Act Book I, printed 1908; EV-0833). The three parishes are already one rectory here; CCEd dates the formal union to 1698 (EV-0834). A church-patronage record, not a land title.
events.source: Llandaff Records vol. 1 (1908), p. 53, archive.org copy

events.event: Williams family occupancy begins, per Mary’s statement (earlier written source awaited) (family origins)

Hearth tax returns of 1671 and 1673 list seven households in the neighbouring parish of Cogan, as cited in the HER entry for the Cogan deserted medieval village (EV-0737). The returns themselves are not read here; no Llandough figure is given.
events.source: Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust HER 1965194, Cogan Deserted Medieval Village (ADS catalogue copy, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: Three Williams rectors in succession serve Leckwith, Llandough and Cogan: Howell (Hoelus) Williams instituted 1689 (died 1714), William (Gulielmus) Williams admitted 1714, Charles Williams instituted 1736 (died 1753) (CCEd location records; EV-0834). Their relation to the Williams of Tŷ Mawr is not checked.
events.source: Clergy of the Church of England Database, location 234489 (archive.org capture)

events.event: An estate map of 1784 of the neighbouring parish of Cogan shows the church with four small cottages around an elongated green running east–west, and a substantial house south of the church, as described in the HER entry (EV-0737). The map’s archive reference and owner are not checked.
events.source: Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust HER 1965194, Cogan Deserted Medieval Village (ADS catalogue copy, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: Estate plans, 1786-1832 (Herbert of White Friars / William Hurst estate) — Estate plans 1786–1832 of lands in Cogan, Llandough-juxta-Penarth, Penarth, St Andrews Major and Sully (Percy Randell collection, Hurst/Herbert estate).
Late 18th-century plan of Ty Mawr farm, Llandough, then 'Gedrych property' (Glamorgan Archives DMAT/279).
events.source: Glamorgan Archives (Canfod catalogue) Glamorgan Archives DMAT/279; Mathew Family of Radyr and Llandaff, Papers (estate plans)

events.event: D. R. Paterson (1934, p. 30) writes that the manor of Cogan, with its mansion of Cogan Pill, stayed with the Herberts until the line ended in heiresses in the mid-18th century and "was ultimately purchased in 1793 by Lord Bute"; he reads the 1545 Herbert rental as making it "very probable" that Cogan manor included lands in Llandough parish (EV-0842). The 1793 conveyance is not checked; this concerns Cogan manor, not Tŷ Mawr.
events.source: D. R. Paterson, 'The Manors of Sully, Cosmeston, Penarth and Cogan', Trans. Cardiff Naturalists' Society LXVII (1934), pp. 17-30 (NLW Welsh Journals scan, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: Calvert Richard Jones releases to the Earl of Bute the manors of Llandough, Cogan, Kibbor and Cardiff (otherwise Whitefriars) and land in the parishes of Llandough-juxta-Penarth and others, 'as in schedule' (Glamorgan Archives catalogue of a later copy). The catalogued schedule names upland farms; no Llandough farm and not Tŷ Mawr (Great House). Shows land, not only manorial rights, in the 1793 purchase; counts against the family case.
events.source: Glamorgan Archives DSA/107/34/11, item 82, copy release (Canfod catalogue entry read 7 Nov 2026; document not seen)

events.event: Plan of Ty Mawr farm, Llandough drawn (c.1800; Glamorgan Archives DXJF/61/12).
events.source: Glamorgan Archives (Canfod catalogue) Glamorgan Archives DXJF/61/12; Corbett Family of Cogan Pill Papers

events.event: Draft mortgage: Herbert Hurst of Gabalva, with the consent of Calvert Richard Jones, charges his moiety of messuages and lands in Llandough-juxta-Penarth and others, and a 'Moiety of Manors of Dinas Powys, Llandough, Cogan, HIghlight and Kibbor', to secure an annuity to William Vaughan. A Hurst half still held after 1793; a draft, execution not shown; Tŷ Mawr not named.
events.source: Glamorgan Archives DART/W/81, draft mortgage (Canfod catalogue entry read 7 Nov 2026; document not seen)

events.event: The Cambrian advertises a Chancery sale (Thomas against Hurst) of freehold estates in Llandough-juxta-Penarth, St Andrews, Cadoxton-juxta-Barry, Merthyr Dyfan and Roath, by auction at the Cardiff Arms Inn on 29 Sep 1813; the Llandough lots are not identified and Tŷ Mawr (Great House) is not named.
events.source: The Cambrian, 11 Sep 1813, p.1 (Welsh Newspapers, National Library of Wales)

events.event: In Chancery (Thomas against Hurst): certified copy report of the sale of William Hurst's freehold estates in Llandough-juxta-Penarth and four other parishes, auctioned at the Cardiff Arms Inn on 29 Sep 1813; lots 12-16 bought by Evan Thomas of Sully. The lots are not described and Tŷ Mawr (Great House) is not named.
events.source: Glamorgan Archives DART/W/82 (Canfod catalogue entry read 8 Nov 2026; document not seen)

events.event: Former National School, Penlan Road / Lewis Road, Llandough built (Coflein NPRN 31824).
events.source: Coflein (RCAHMW National Monuments Record of Wales) NPRN 31824; grid ST1674073140

events.event: Stewart’s survey of the Bute estates, plan 19 “Cedfin or Ty Mawr Farm”: 139a 3r 8p, including 20a 2r 35p of wood; occupier read as John Gedrick; 10a 3r 39p of “late Thos. Williams” land added (Glamorgan Archives DB/E/1) (EV-0211)
Survey of the Bute estates, plan 19 “Cedfin or Ty Mawr Farm”, 139a 3r 8p
Bute estate survey by David Stewart maps 'Cedfin alias Ty Mawr farm; in Llandough' (Glamorgan Archives DB/E/1-2).
events.source: Glamorgan Archives (Canfod catalogue) Glamorgan Archives DB/E/1-2; Bute, Glamorgan Estate

events.source: Glamorgan Archives (Canfod catalogue) Glamorgan Archives P35/10; Llandough-juxta-Penarth Civil Parish Records

events.event: Tithe apportionment for Llandough, Cogan and Leckwith, schedule canvas 23: the landowner column reads “Manor lord of the (Marquess of Bute)” only for plots 319–322 (Leckwith moors pasture, occupier William Thomas), 4 of the 577 indexed rows. The Tŷ Mawr (Great House) plots, 209 “Courtyard &c” among them, carry the other form, “Bute the Marquess of”. The schedule does not explain the difference.
events.source: National Library of Wales, tithe apportionment Llandough, Cogan and Leckwith (NLW 4542756), schedule canvas 23, rows 319–334, read against the NLW Places of Wales index (577 rows) 6 Nov 2026 · EV-0215

events.event: Tithe plan and apportionment for Llandough-juxta-Penarth parish (Glamorgan Archives P35).
events.source: Glamorgan Archives (Canfod catalogue) Glamorgan Archives P35

also.source: Glamorgan Archives (Canfod catalogue) Glamorgan Archives P35/9; Llandough-juxta-Penarth Civil Parish Records

events.event: The Cardiff and Merthyr Guardian reports a ploughing match (1 Dec 1847) for the sons and servants of farmers in Leckwith, Llandough and Cogan; a prize goes to “William Williams, eldest son of Mr. J. … of the Great House Farm, Landough”: the name Great House Farm in print by 1847.
events.source: The Cardiff and Merthyr Guardian, 4 Dec 1847, p.3, 'Agricultural Emulation' (Welsh Newspapers)

events.event: Cogan Pill (now Barons Court, Llandough community) is 'Restored and remodelled c 1850 by H S Corbett, relative and agent of the Marquess of Bute, as a house for himself'; Cadw's list text records that the former Herbert hall house had earlier been 'later becoming a farmhouse'. A separate house, not a Tŷ Mawr parcel.
events.source: Cadw listed building full report 15765, 'Barons Court PH' (read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: At St Mary's Church, Cardiff, William, second son of Mr John Williams of Great House Farm, Landough, marries Miss Martha Rees of Cardiff (family notice in The Cardiff and Merthyr Guardian, 21 Aug 1852). Read from the OCR text; the page image is not checked.
events.source: The Cardiff and Merthyr Guardian, 21 Aug 1852, p.3, Family Notices (Welsh Newspapers, National Library of Wales)

events.event: John Williams succeeds his father in the occupancy of the farm, per a 1904 press report: “He succeeded his father in the occupancy of the farm in 1855” (Cardiff Times, 16 Jul 1904, which calls him “of Llandough Farm”; that he is the Great House John Williams is an inference) (Cardiff Times 1904; EV-0224)

The Penarth Harbour Dock and Railway Act is passed on 27 July 1857 and work on the dock begins in 1859; the Lower Marsh and the Cogan Pill area are "lost when work started on the Dock excavations in 1859", as written in Alan Thorne's Place names of Penarth (1997) (EV-0819). Penarth side of the Ely; the Act's deposited plans and book of reference are not checked.
events.source: Alan Thorne, Place names of Penarth (1997) (archive.org lending copy, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: A London Gazette notice for the Penarth Waterworks Bill proposes "A reservoir in the parish of Llandough" about five chains south-west of "The Merry Harrier Inn", where the road from Dinas Powis to Cogan Pill crosses the road from Cogan to Llandough, with mains through Llandough, Cogan and Penarth (EV-0823). A book of reference naming owners, lessees and occupiers was to be deposited; it is not checked.
events.source: The London Gazette, 26 Nov 1858, issue 22204, p. 5159

events.event: A London Gazette notice for the Cardiff Water Works Bill describes a reservoir "lately constructed by the Company at Cogan Pill Farm, in the parish of Llandough" (the Cogan Pill Reservoir) and a new "Llandough Reservoir" "in a field in the occupation of Thomas Rees", near the road from Leckwith to Dinas Powis and "about 600 yards westward of Llandough Church" (EV-0824). Thomas Rees is the separate Llandough Farm occupier; no Tŷ Mawr (Great House) parcel is named. The deposited plans and book of reference are not checked.
events.source: The London Gazette, 25 Nov 1859, issue 22329, pp. 4375-4376

events.event: Amy Williams, “relict of the late Mr. John Williams, Great House farm”, dies at Llandough, aged 65 (EV-0246)
Cardiff Times and Cardiff and Merthyr Guardian, 30 Dec 1864: death of Amy, “relict of the late Mr. John Williams, Great House farm”

Webster's directory of Bristol and Glamorgan (1865, p.443) describes Llandough near Penarth: 'The soil belongs to the Marquis of Bute, who is also lord of the manor'. Its resident list (p.444) has 'Williams, John, farmer' and 'Williams, John, lime burner', with no farm named. A directory statement about the whole parish, not a title record; it counts against the family case.
events.source: Webster & Co.'s Postal and Commercial Directory of the City of Bristol and County of Glamorgan (1865), pp. 443-444 (text layer read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: Present St Dochdwy's Church, Llandough consecrated; its c.1820 predecessor moved and rebuilt at Leckwith.

also.source: Coflein (RCAHMW National Monuments Record of Wales) NPRN 227363; grid ST1680073270

events.event: Harrod's directory of Glamorganshire (1866, p.463) repeats the 1865 figures for Llandough near Penarth (600 acres, rateable value £1,327): 'The land belongs to the Marquis of Bute, who is lord of the manor'; residents again include 'Williams John, farmer' and 'Williams John, lime burner'. Likely the same statement as 1865, not an independent one; counts against the family case.
events.source: Harrod & Co.'s Postal and Commercial Directory of Glamorganshire (1866), p. 463 (text layer read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: The National Gazetteer (1868) entry for Llandough-juxta-Penarth: limestone quarries, the church of St Dochdwy with 'the remains of an ancient cross', and 'A farm here was formerly the seat of the Herbert family'. The farm is not named (most likely Cogan Pill, not checked); no dated form of the Tŷ Mawr name.
events.source: The National Gazetteer: a topographical dictionary of the British Islands (London, 1868), vol. 2 (Internet Archive text, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: The 1871 census for Llandough juxta Penarth (RG10/5368, p.3, schedule 14) records John Williams, head, 43, born Llandough, “Farmer 110 Acres, Emp 2 Men”, with his wife Mary (41) and daughters, at the house the enumerator names “Great House Farm”. Read from the FreeCEN transcription; the page image is not checked.
events.source: TNA RG10/5368 p.3 sched.14 (1871 census), FreeCEN transcription

events.event: Glebe land in Llandough parish conveyed as a school site (Glamorgan Archives P35CW/9).
events.source: Glamorgan Archives (Canfod catalogue) Glamorgan Archives P35CW/9; Llandough-juxta-Penarth with Leckwith Ecclesiastical Parish Records

events.event: Llandough poor rate: John Williams rated for glebe land, owner Rev. H.H. Rickards (rate book, reference pending) (EV-0212)
Worrall’s Directory lists “Williams John, Great house” in Llandough parish; Slater’s 1868 and 1880, Owen’s 1887 and 1891 and the 1901 Cardiff Directory list him at Great House as well (EV-0225)
Worrall's Directory lists a Williams farmer at 'Great house', Llandough parish (Penarth section).
events.source: University of Leicester Special Collections – Historical Directories Worrall's Directory of South Wales, 1875 - Page 324

events.event: The parishes of Penarth, Cogan and Llandough are merged into the Penarth Local Board (population 6,228 by 1881). From then the local board, not the parish, held rates, highways and sanitary matters for Llandough. Primary order not yet read.
events.source: Wikipedia, 'Penarth' (citing S. Williams, South Glamorgan: A County History, 1975), re-read 3 Nov 2026; the 1875 Local Government Board order not read

events.event: NLW Bute deeds D153/4–8, catalogue entry: “land (33 a.), formerly part of Great House Farm, for the Llandough Limeworks (33 a.), 1876-1912 (D153/4-8). Plan engrossed on D153/3 (1875) and 4 (1876).” The deeds, their parties and the parcel are unread (EV-0291; SC-21; Llandough Limeworks)
Bute deeds: “land (33 a.), formerly part of Great House Farm, for the Llandough Limeworks (33 a.), 1876-1912”; plan engrossed on D153/3 (1875) and 4 (1876)

Llandough poor rate: John Williams rated for a farm, owner Lord Bute, c. 76a, gross £41 0s (same sequence in the rate of 20 Aug 187?, year unread); Lord Bute rated for woods in hand, 32a 3r 39p; Daniel Thomas & Son rated for a lime kiln and quarry (EV-0212)
Bute serves notice to quit (Mary’s statement) (notice to quit)
Mary (Nancy) Williams’s statement reports a sale of the farmhouse/buildings and about 10 acres to Daniel Thomas, with about 9 acres retained by Bute; original deed/plan missing (1877 sale, plan)

Date reported for a lease to John Williams in Mary (Nancy) Williams’s account; no matching Llandough instrument has been identified. The checked DBDT/79/1 item is a 2 May 1877 lease for Pembroke Terrace, Cardiff; other similarly named Cardiff lease references remain catalogue leads, not verified Llandough evidence (SC-20; 1877 Agreement). A Bute Trustees counterpart lease of this date to John Williams, builder, of System Street, Roath, for a plot in Clyde Street, Roath, is photographed; it is not the farm (EV-0213; Excluded).
Ordnance Survey surveys Glamorgan six-inch sheet XLVII (Cardiff/Penarth area) 1878–79; published 1885.
events.source: National Library of Scotland – Ordnance Survey Six-inch England and Wales Glamorgan Sheet XLVII, surveyed 1878–1879, published 1885 (first edition six-inch); Llandough's position on the sheet not visually checked

events.event: OS large-scale Glamorgan sheets XLVII/2–15 surveyed c.1878 cover Llandough-juxta-Penarth (council copies, Glamorgan Archives DCVG/PL/1).
events.source: Glamorgan Archives (Canfod catalogue) Glamorgan Archives DCVG/PL/1; Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council, Planning and Environmental Services Department

events.event: ‘Armour’ reported found under the floor of the rear wing of Great House; thought to be the medieval ironwork from Llandough now at the National Museum.

The 1881 census records John Williams, 53, “Farmer of 170[? or 120] ac.”, with his wife Mary and children at “Llandough Home Farm”, Llandough (RG11/5288 p.2). On our case’s reading, the census mixed up the Llandough farm with Great House Farm, so this is Great House Farm under another name (EV-0224)

Glamorgan Archives' catalogue of the Cardiff Poor Law Union records lists parish rate books for the three neighbouring parishes: Llandough 1882-1902 (UC/73, five volumes, with no volume between Nov 1884 and May 1896), Cogan 1895-1902 (UC/72) and Penarth 1880-1902 (UC/74), continuing the 1872-1876 Llandough rate books (EV-0848; EV-0212). The volumes are not read, so the Great House entries in them are not checked.
events.source: Glamorgan Archives catalogue (Canfod), Cardiff Poor Law Union records UC/72-UC/74 (read 7 Nov 2026)

Owen's Cardiff Directory lists a Williams at Great House farm, Llandough, Penarth.

Apples taken from “the orchard of Great House Farm … the property of John Williams”, reached “over the hedge from the railway”; John Williams junior gives evidence (Barry Dock News, 16 Aug 1889) (EV-0279)
Barry Dock News, 16 Aug 1889, p.2: apples taken from “the orchard of Great House Farm … the property of John Williams”; orchard reached “over the hedge from the railway”

Andrew Road is cut into the western escarpment of the Cogan glacial bowl in the 1890s, "the intention being to shorten the route from Cogan to Llandough", as written in Alan Thorne's Place names of Penarth (1997, p. 11) (EV-0740). The book gives no primary source; the Penarth highway records are not checked, and its "owner of the parishes" wording is the book's.
events.source: Alan Thorne, Place names of Penarth (1997), p. 11 (archive.org lending copy, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: Three geese taken from “Mr. John Williams, Great House Farm, Llandough”; the court report is contemporary evidence of his occupancy (press 1891)
newspaper cutting (title not printed): “Newspaper report: reported theft of geese from Great House Farm, Llandough (1891)”
South Wales Echo: “ THEFT OF GEESE AT LLANDOUGH” — Court report: three geese taken on 11 Nov 1891 from John Williams of Great House Farm, Llandough; police evidence heard.
South Wales Daily News: “ THEFT OF GEESE AT LLANDOUGH” — Same court case reported in the South Wales Daily News: geese of John Williams, Great House Farm.
South Wales Star reports geese taken, “the property of Mr. John Williams, Great House Farm, Llandough, on November 11, 1891” (South Wales Star 1892; EV-0224)
South Wales Star: “LLANDOUGH.” — Penarth magistrates hearing on the geese taken from John Williams, Great House Farm, Llandough, in Nov 1891.

A deed of exchange of 27 September 1893 between the trustees of the will of the late marquess of Bute and the marquess covers lands in Leckwith, "Llandough-juxta-Barry", Cogan and six other parishes, with a detailed schedule and plans (Glamorgan Archives DB/33/1-2, catalogue entry; EV-0843). The schedule and plans are not seen (missing record MR-0067), so the fields involved, and which Llandough is meant, are not checked.
events.source: Glamorgan Archives, Bute Glamorgan Estates catalogue (GB 0214 DB), DB/33/1-2 (catalogue PDF on TNA Discovery, read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: Penarth Urban District Council, formed in 1894 from the Penarth Local Board of Health, is responsible for the parishes of Penarth, Cogan and Llandough juxta Penarth until 31 March 1974, when it merges into the Vale of Glamorgan District Council; its minutes, deed registers and building regulation plans (1877-c1973, incomplete) are at Glamorgan Archives, UDPE (EV-0850).
events.source: Glamorgan Archives catalogue (Canfod), Penarth Urban District Council records UDPE, fonds description (read 7 Nov 2026)

events.event: Rev. F. E. Williams inducted as rector of Llandough, Leckwith and Cogan (Bute patron of the living): a different Williams, not the Great House family (EV-0281)
Swine fever at Llandough: “Five pigs belonging to Mr Williams, Great House, have been slaughtered” (Barry Dock News, 3 Aug 1894) (EV-0247)
Barry Dock News and Glamorgan Gazette, 3 Aug 1894: swine fever; five pigs of “Mr Williams, Great House” slaughtered

Obituary of J. E. Billups: “the Penarth Brickworks, which were started by him” (South Wales Daily News, 26 Nov 1896, p.6). A published brickworks history places the Llandough brickworks “next door” to the lime works “by 1899”, Billups Brick Co Ltd proprietor, “Llandough Brick Co by 1923”, “disused” by 1947 (secondary) (EV-0292)

industrialgwent: “Llandough Lime Works and the brickworks next door: “owned in 1871 by D Thomas and Son”; brickworks “opened next door by 1899”, J. E. Billups, “Llandough Brick Co by 1923”, “disused” by 1947…”
George Kemp’s diary (Marconi’s assistant): Lavernock pole “107 ft”, Flat Holm “110 ft”, apparatus left “at Penarth”; no mention of Great House Farm (EV-0256)
Evening Express: “Wireless Telegraphy. Marconi Invention Tested at Lavernock”

Marconi’s wireless trials with the Post Office at Lavernock Point, Flat Holm and Brean Down. The receiving pole at Lavernock was put up by “Mr. Williams (of the engineering department, Cardiff)” (Evening Express, 15 May 1897, p.4, identified 19 Oct 2026 as the cutting EV-0011). The first Brean Down tape is dated 18 May 1897. Marconi left England on 5 Jul 1897. Link to Great House: evidence being added. (EV-0248; press 1897)
events.source: Legal Wiki, Master Timeline · EV-0011, EV-0248

events.event: Evening Express: “Marconi in Wales, April–July 1897: the contemporary Welsh press record (Lavernock, Flat Holm, Brean Down)”
1900 map of Llandough shows 'Ty-mawr' (Great House) beside St Dochdwy's Church.

Western Ground Rents gives c.109 acres of Leckwith Woods to Cardiff council (offered and accepted 1940, completed April 1942; secondary source) Working theories (evidence pending): the 1940–42 woods gift and Parcel A. Each theory is stated as a theory, with its support and the record that would test it. Each rests on the dated records named and on our case’s reading of them; evidence being added.Provenance of the plan of the Williams parcel (corrected 20 Oct 2026): date and origin unknown; disclosed 2026. Our case links it to the 1877 Daniel Thomas & Son agreement . It is the only known source for the three-way split of Parcel A, much as Parcel B is known from the 1939 occupancy plan. See the plan.T1 (theory): the woods gift to Cardiff took in the woodland third of Parcel A. Support: the gift was “110 acres of wooded land at Leckwith” (Western Mail, 14 Sep 1940, p.5; press search snippet), about 109 acres in the council’s own history (Cardiff Parks; EV-0220); Parcel A’s woods are “practically Leckwith” and are now held by the Forest of Cardiff charity (our case, 20 Oct 2026; charity 1002867; woodland title WA735527, transferred 10 Nov 1994: EV-0136, GHF-E149). Test: the April 1942 WGR → Cardiff conveyance and its plan, laid over the c.1841 tithe parcel 266 “Wood” and the WA735527 plan; Cardiff’s Parks Committee minutes of 15 Oct 1940 to 15 Apr 1942 (Glamorgan Archives BC/C/6/78–80). The plan will show whether the gift’s ground reaches the woods beside the farm, some of which straddle the Llandough–Leckwith line, or lies higher on Leckwith Hill.
